answer.rationale: The binding constraints are asymmetric: the 18% cost mandate is painful but recoverable, whereas a supply gap at 94% committed volume with no buffer is not. That rules out switch_primary_vendor as the single decision this cycle (a 14-day window is too short to qualify and ramp a new primary on a line with no slack) and rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback is not available here \u2014 this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring is a de facto supply lapse). add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right long-run structural move but does not deliver the mandated in-year cost reduction and does not by itself secure the expiring primary contract. That leaves negotiate_terms, but not the memory_c4 pattern \u2014 the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, so re-running a price benchmark is the one negotiation that is known to fail. The live lever is memory_c6: restructuring on term length and volume commitment to unlock tiered pricing, plus payment-terms and scope adjustments, which reduces TCO without reopening headline price and secures continuity past day 85. I am verifying memory_c6 because it is the sole load-bearing basis for this action and I need the original record to know whether the volume pricing came from term length itself or from a specific volume threshold Halden may no longer clear, and what the actual realized unit-cost delta was (whether it plausibly approaches 18% or only a fraction of it). I am verifying memory_c2 because it is the strongest cost case for the alternative I am declining, and I need to know the switched component's criticality, the actual onboarding duration, and whether the line had buffer at the time \u2014 if onboarding was genuinely fast on a comparable critical part, switching becomes materially more defensible and I should reconsider. Uncertainty I am explicitly not resolving: every inherited memory here reads as a success, which is a survivorship signature \u2014 the failed switches, failed negotiations and lapsed renewals are almost certainly not in this record, so the base rates implied by these six entries are optimistic and should not be treated as calibrated. Downstream value risk: a multi-year commitment buys unit cost by spending exactly the optionality that memory_c3's dual-sourcing logic depends on, deepening lock-in with a supplier that has just demonstrated it can refuse to move on price. I therefore intend to negotiate a term structure that preserves a qualification carve-out and volume headroom for a second source at the next review, rather than a clean multi-year exclusive, and I will scope this as a standard commitment rather than a maximal-length one even if longer terms price better. If memory_c6's discount turns out to be threshold-driven and Halden cannot clear the threshold, or if memory_c2's switch precedent proves to be a comparable critical part with genuinely short onboarding, I will revisit before committing.
